about: The one list of Will Cook's websites, films and repositories. The home page at wcook04.github.io is built from it, and each website keeps a copy for its own header, footer and film slots. Edit this file, then follow README.md, 'Add a released film'.

owner.name: Will Cook
owner.lede: I’ve been using AI to do maths research and build software. As it produces more complicated work, I also want to make that work easier for other people to understand.
invitation: These videos show what I’ve learned to build. I’d love to put those skills to use on other problems. I’m looking for work, an internship, fellowship or funding, and I’m very open to working together. If there’s a problem you think I should try, please let me know.
If something doesn’t make sense, or you spot a mistake, please let me know. If your feedback leads to a change, I’d be happy to credit you, with your permission.

sites.name: Plectis Mathematics
sites.purpose: Research with AI on eight Erdős problems: papers, Lean proofs of partial results, and the approaches that failed.
sites.status: Each problem page says whether the original question is still open.
sites.capture_caption: The front page of Plectis Mathematics, open at problem #68.

sites.name: Lean Exposition
sites.purpose: Three explanations of one theorem about the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model of interacting spins. Click a linked statement to see its Lean code beside the text.
sites.status: The three papers are drafts. AI agents made the links to the Lean, and the site lists each Lean run and the statements it covers.
sites.capture_caption: The short paper at Theorem 1, beside the graph of its argument.

sites.name: Proof Reader
sites.purpose: Read a research paper beside its authors’ Lean proof. Click a linked statement to open the corresponding code, or explore the diagram of proof steps.
sites.status: The first paper is Contextual Embeddings by Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang. AI agents made the links to the Lean; the authors have not reviewed them.
sites.capture_caption: Contextual Embeddings on the left page, with the graph of its Lean proof and the exact lines on the right.

sites.name: Quartic Reader
sites.purpose: Read OpenAI’s paper on a nearly quartic gap between randomized and quantum query complexity, and two explanations of its proof. As you scroll, a panel beside the text shows the Lean declarations linked to the paragraph you are reading.
sites.status: The theorem and construction are OpenAI’s. I made the explanations and the Lean proof with AI. Lean accepts the proof; only AI has reviewed the links between paragraphs and Lean.
sites.capture_caption: The general reader beside the graph of the Lean proof, following the paragraph being read.

sites.name: Plectis Atlas
sites.purpose: Read OpenAI’s maths papers alongside the reports that outside groups wrote about their claims and proofs.
sites.capture_caption: The Atlas map: each circle is a subject and each dot a family of papers.

sites.name: Practical Formal Verification

routes.label: Which proofs and tests cover each one

sites.purpose: 88 Python components from my research system. In twelve of them, Dafny proves that a small computation follows its written rules, and the running code matches the proved code.
sites.capture_caption: The system map: the 88 components in their seven families.

sites.name: Zenith
sites.purpose: Experiments testing whether an AI code tester finds more bugs after it is shown the bugs it missed, and whether records of missed bugs help AI models repair code.
sites.status: Small studies. The repository states the limits of each one.
sites.capture_caption: The opening of the Zenith paper.

sites.name: Code Ontology Bridge
sites.purpose: Exports a Python repository’s files, functions, calls and imports to a database, with a semantic model that NVIDIA Auto Ontology’s SQL agent can query.
sites.status: A study compares the agent’s answers with and without the model on 48 questions about four repositories. The questions were written without reference to the model, and every question, answer and failed run is published.
sites.capture_caption: Calls followed backwards from a function, with a callback reference shown dashed.

projects.name: Agent Trace
projects.purpose: Lets a coding agent read earlier Codex and Claude Code chats, including messages, commands and command output. It runs on your computer as an MCP server.

projects.name: Safety Core
projects.purpose: Keeps a coding agent’s rules in one file and marks which rules are only written instructions and which also have a hook that blocks commands the rule forbids.

projects.name: One Checkout
projects.purpose: Commits one agent’s change in Git while another agent’s unfinished edits in the same files stay uncommitted.

projects.name: Code Map
projects.purpose: A map of my code: open a file to read its saved description, then follow the function calls between files.
projects.status: Not released; the video shows it in use.

index_groups.title: Software and experiments with AI agents

repos.name: plectis-erdos
repos.description: Papers, Lean proofs, experiments and open questions from the research on eight Erdős problems, and papers on how the research was done.

repos.name: plectis-erdos-lean
repos.description: Lean 4 source for the eight problems. Comparator accepted selected proofs against separately written statements, and Palomar, an online proof registry, reran some of them.

repos.name: lean-exposition
repos.description: The three papers, the Lean they link to at a fixed version, and the source of the reading website.

repos.name: proof-reader
repos.description: Each paper is one folder, and any paper with public Lean can be added. A program compares the site’s text with the PDF word for word.

repos.name: plectis-atlas
repos.description: The Atlas website’s source: OpenAI’s maths papers, their Lean statements, and outside groups’ reports credited to their authors.

repos.name: practical-formal-verification
repos.description: The 88 Python components, their Dafny proofs and saved results, and worked examples.

repos.name: plectis-zenith
repos.description: Code, data and paper for the experiments on showing an AI tester the bugs it missed, and the code-repair studies.

repos.name: safety-core
repos.description: A rule file for coding agents and the hooks that block commands a rule forbids.

repos.name: one-checkout
repos.description: Commit one agent’s fix without including another agent’s unfinished edits.

repos.name: agent-trace-mechanism
repos.description: A history reader and MCP server for Codex and Claude Code that runs on your computer. You choose which chats an agent can read, and the agent gets a compact transcript or the full tool activity.

repos.name: code-ontology-bridge
repos.description: Exports a Python repository’s files, functions, calls, imports and docstrings to DuckDB with a native Auto Ontology semantic model.

repos.name: quartic-query-lean
repos.description: The Lean proof of OpenAI’s nearly quartic separation, three written explanations of the argument, and the reader website’s source.

film_groups.title: Tools for working with AI agents

films.title: Introduction (V3): I still want to understand what AI builds
films.description: I use AI for maths research and software, and build interfaces so other people can follow the results.

films.title: Introduction (V1, older version): How the projects fit together
films.description: An older introduction. Watch the latest Introduction (V3) from the home page. I go through the maths, the code map, how I make these videos, and the tools I use to manage the agents. Then some research into how the agents could improve their own way of working.

films.title: Maths Map: eight Erdős problems on one map
films.description: I use one problem, Erdős #257, to show where its proof, papers and explanation video are on the Maths Map.

films.title: Erdős #257: why some infinite sums cannot be fractions
films.description: I explain a known irrationality result for Erdős #257, starting with 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, and so on.

films.title: Lean Exposition: read a maths paper beside its argument map
films.description: I show how to read a maths explanation beside a map of its assumptions, results and sources.

films.title: Spin glasses: how different can two nearly best answers be?
films.description: I explain how two nearly best arrangements of magnets can differ, starting with four arrows.

films.title: Atlas: why two people gave one OpenAI maths paper different verdicts on its completeness
films.description: I compare two reports on an OpenAI maths paper about pi that disagree on whether its proof is complete.

films.title: Formal verification: what does this check actually prove?
films.description: On a map of the 88 Python components, I show what each Dafny proof and saved result covers.

films.title: Zenith: I showed an AI tester the bugs it missed
films.description: I test whether an AI code tester catches more bugs after seeing a record of its earlier misses.

films.title: Safety Core: my AI agent made up a setting to pass a test
films.description: I give a coding agent written rules and command-blocking hooks, then record what it does to get past a failing test.

films.title: One Checkout: when Claude is done and Codex is still editing
films.description: I show how to commit one fix while another agent's unfinished edits stay in the same file.

films.title: CodeMap: finding my way through code written with AI
films.description: I follow a code search from a file's saved description to the function and the code that calls it.

films.title: Introduction (V2, older version): Using AI for maths research and software
films.description: An older introduction. Watch the latest Introduction (V3) from the home page. In this video I introduce the projects and explain how they fit together, from computer-checked proofs and papers to maps and videos you can follow yourself.
